title: Applications of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
learningObjective: Solve application problems using exponential and logarithmic equations.

faqs.question: What makes a word problem an "exponential" or "logarithmic" application?
faqs.answer: Look for a quantity that changes by a constant PERCENT or FACTOR over equal time intervals, rather than by a constant amount. Phrases like "grows by 5% per year," "doubles every 3 hours," "decays at a continuous rate of 17%," or "compounded monthly" are all signals that you're dealing with exponential change — the same constant-ratio idea from EL1, just embedded in a real context.

faqs.question: What is Newton's Law of Cooling, and what does each part of the formula represent?
faqs.answer:
Newton's Law of Cooling models how an object's temperature changes over time as it adjusts toward the temperature of its surroundings.
Formula

\[ T(x) = ab^x + d \]

\( a \) is the difference between the starting temperature and the surrounding temperature, \( b \) is the decay factor, \( x \) is elapsed time, and \( d \) is the surrounding (ambient) temperature — which is also the model's horizontal asymptote.

The coffee cools quickly at first, then levels off as it approaches room temperature — never quite reaching it.

faqs.question: What is the compound interest formula, and what does each variable represent?
faqs.answer:
The compound interest formula models an account balance that earns interest at regular intervals throughout the year.
Formula

\[ A(t) = P\left(1+\dfrac{r}{n}\right)^{nt} \]

\( A(t) \) is the account value after \( t \) years, \( P \) is the principal (starting amount), \( r \) is the annual interest rate as a decimal, and \( n \) is the number of times interest compounds per year.

faqs.question: What is continuous growth/decay, and how is it different from periodic compounding?
faqs.answer:
Continuous growth or decay assumes a quantity is changing constantly, at every single instant, rather than at set intervals (yearly, monthly, etc.) — it's the limiting case of compounding more and more frequently, all the way down to continuously. It always uses base \( e \), since \( e \) is precisely the constant that arises from that continuous-compounding limit (EL1).
Formulas

General continuous growth/decay: \( A(t) = ae^{rt} \)

Continuous compounding (finance): \( A(t) = Pe^{rt} \)

faqs.question: How do I know whether an application involves growth or decay?
faqs.answer: Check the sign or size of the rate. For \( A(t)=ae^{rt} \): if \( r>0 \), it's growth; if \( r<0 \), it's decay. For \( f(x)=ab^x \): if \( b>1 \), it's growth; if \( 0<b<1 \), it's decay — the exact same rule from EL1, now applied inside a real-world context.

faqs.question: How do I build an exponential model from a word problem when I'm given a starting value and one other data point?
faqs.answer:
The starting value IS your \( a \). Plug the other data point into \( f(x)=ab^x \) along with that \( a \), then solve algebraically for \( b \).
Worked Example

In 2006, 80 deer were introduced. By 2012 (6 years later), the population reached 180.

Initial value: \( a=80 \)

Plug in: \( 180=80b^6 \) → \( b^6=2.25 \) → \( b=2.25^{1/6}\approx 1.1447 \)

Model: \( N(t)=80(1.1447)^t \)

faqs.question: How do I build an exponential model from a word problem when I'm given two data points, neither at time zero?
faqs.answer: Use the exact same method from EL1 for finding an equation from two points: divide the two output values to find the common ratio over however many steps apart they are, take the appropriate root to find \( b \), then work backward (or forward) to find \( a \).

faqs.question: How do I use the compound interest formula to find the value of an account after a given number of years?
faqs.answer:
Identify \( P \), \( r \), and \( n \) from the problem, plug them in along with the given \( t \), and evaluate.
Worked Example

$5,000 invested at 4% annual interest, compounded quarterly, for 10 years.

\( P=5000, r=0.04, n=4, t=10 \)

\( A(10) = 5000\left(1+\dfrac{0.04}{4}\right)^{4(10)} \approx \$7{,}446.55 \)

faqs.question: How do I use the continuous compounding/growth formula, and when do I use it instead of the periodic formula?
faqs.answer:
Use the continuous formula \( A(t)=Pe^{rt} \) whenever a problem specifically says "compounded continuously" or describes continuous growth/decay (like most natural growth and decay processes, e.g. radioactive decay or bacteria growth) — otherwise, use the periodic formula from faq-3 with whatever compounding frequency \( n \) is stated.
Worked Example

$1,000 invested at 10% compounded continuously for 1 year.

\( A(1)=1000e^{0.10(1)} \approx \$1{,}105.17 \)

faqs.question: How do I solve an application problem for time, like "when will this population reach a certain size?"
faqs.answer:
Set the model equal to the target value, then solve for \( t \) using logarithms — exactly the EL6 equation-solving method, just with meaning attached to every variable.
Worked Example

Using \( N(t)=80(1.1447)^t \) from faq-6, when does the population reach 250?

\( 250 = 80(1.1447)^t \) → \( 3.125 = 1.1447^t \)

Take log of both sides: \( t = \dfrac{\log(3.125)}{\log(1.1447)} \approx 8.43 \) years

faqs.question: How do I solve a Newton's Law of Cooling problem for the time it takes to reach a certain temperature?
faqs.answer:
Set \( T(x) \) equal to the target temperature, isolate the exponential piece by subtracting the surrounding temperature \( d \) first, then take the log of both sides and solve for \( x \) — same method as faq-10, just with the extra vertical-shift step to undo first.
Worked Example

Using \( T(x)=70(0.80)^x+20 \), when does the coffee reach 35°C?

\( 35=70(0.80)^x+20 \) → \( 15=70(0.80)^x \) → \( 0.2143=0.80^x \)

\( x=\dfrac{\log(0.2143)}{\log(0.80)}\approx 6.9 \) minutes

faqs.question: How do I interpret the asymptote of a Newton's Law of Cooling model in context?
faqs.answer: The asymptote is exactly the surrounding (ambient) temperature — the value the object's temperature approaches but never quite reaches as time goes on. This is EL2's vertical-shift rule showing up in a real context: the \( +d \) in the formula shifts the entire decay curve up to sit right on top of the room's temperature, rather than decaying all the way to zero.

faqs.question: How do I set up and solve a continuous decay problem, like radioactive decay?
faqs.answer:
Use \( A(t)=ae^{rt} \) with a NEGATIVE rate \( r \) (since it's decay), plug in the given information, and solve for whatever's missing using the same log-based method.
Worked Example

Radon-222 decays continuously at 17.3% per day. How much of a 100 mg sample remains after 3 days?

\( A(t)=100e^{-0.173t} \)

\( A(3)=100e^{-0.173(3)} \approx 58.35 \) mg

faqs.question: How does everything from EL1–EL6 come together in this section?
faqs.answer: This section is the payoff for the entire chapter. EL1 gave you the exponential model and how to build one from data. EL2 gave you the asymptote and shift behavior that explains Newton's Law of Cooling's leveling-off shape. EL3 and EL4 gave you logarithms and their graphs. EL5 gave you the properties needed to manipulate these equations. EL6 gave you the actual technique — taking logs of both sides — for solving for a variable trapped in an exponent. Every single piece from this chapter shows up somewhere in a real application here.

faqs.question: Why do these application skills matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Exponential and logarithmic models are how professionals in finance, biology, chemistry, medicine, and public policy actually describe and predict real change — compound interest projections, drug dosage decay in the bloodstream, population and epidemic modeling, and radiometric dating all rely on exactly the skills built in this chapter. Being able to build a model from real data and then solve it for a specific target is one of the most directly applicable skills in this entire course.

guided.title: Practice Building a Model from a Word Problem
guided.prompt: I'm learning to build an exponential model from a word problem. Give me a scenario with a starting value and one other data point (like a population at two different times), and walk me through finding the growth or decay factor and writing the full model. Give me a few more practice problems and check my work.

guided.title: Practice the Compound Interest Formula
guided.prompt: I'm learning to use the compound interest formula. Give me a scenario with a principal, interest rate, and compounding frequency, and ask me to find the account value after a given number of years. Then give me a scenario where I need to solve for time instead, and walk me through that direction too.

guided.title: Practice Newton's Law of Cooling
guided.prompt: I'm learning to use Newton's Law of Cooling. Give me a scenario with a starting temperature, a surrounding temperature, and a decay factor, and ask me to find the temperature after a given time. Then give me a scenario where I need to solve for the time instead, given a target temperature.

guided.title: Compare Periodic and Continuous Models
guided.prompt: I'm trying to understand when to use the periodic compound interest formula versus the continuous growth formula. Can you give me a few scenarios and ask me to identify which formula applies to each one, based on the wording used? Then check my reasoning and help me understand any I got wrong.

guided.title: Connect the Whole EL Chapter to One Application
guided.prompt: I've learned exponential functions, their graphs, logarithms, their graphs, log properties, and equation solving throughout this chapter. Can you walk me through one complete real-world application problem — like the deer population example — and point out exactly which skill from which earlier section I'm using at each step?

paths.label: EL7: Applications of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
paths.sectionLabel: EL7, Applications of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
paths.intro: Builds to the EL7 check: compound interest, population growth, depreciation, and half-life, finding an amount at a given time and the time for a given amount.

stages.desc: Two quick reviews EL7 leans on: percents as growth factors and solving exponential equations (EL6). Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Percents and growth factors
stops.target: Change a percent to a decimal (\(4.5\% = 0.045\)). Growth by \(r\) means multiplying by \(1 + r\); decay by \(r\) means multiplying by \(1 - r\). For compounding, the rate per period is \(\tfrac{r}{n}\).
stops.cold: (a) Write \(3.25\%\) as a decimal. (b) What is the growth factor for 4% growth per year? (c) For 3.25% compounded quarterly, what is \(\tfrac{r}{n}\)?
stops.coldPlain: (a) Write 3.25% as a decimal. (b) Growth factor for 4% growth per year? (c) For 3.25% compounded quarterly, what is r/n?
stops.solution: Move the decimal two places left: 3.25% = 0.0325. Growing by 4% keeps 100% and adds 4%: factor 1.04. Quarterly means n = 4: 0.0325/4 = 0.008125.
stops.mistake: Using 3.25 instead of 0.0325, or 1.4 instead of 1.04.
stops.again: (a) A boat loses 4% of its value each year. What is the yearly factor? (b) For 6% compounded monthly, what are \(n\) and \(\tfrac{r}{n}\)?
stops.reflect: How do you tell whether to use \(1 + r\) or \(1 - r\)?

stops.title: Solve for an exponent
stops.target: Recall from EL6: isolate the power, then use logs. \(b^t = c\) gives \(t = \dfrac{\ln c}{\ln b}\).
stops.cold: Solve \(1.05^t = 2\). Round to four decimal places.
stops.coldPlain: Solve 1.05^t = 2. Round to four decimal places.
stops.solution: Take ln of both sides: t ln 1.05 = ln 2, so t = ln 2 / ln 1.05, about 14.2067.
stops.reflect: What do you always do before taking a log?

stages.desc: Every EL7 scenario asks two kinds of question: given the time, find the amount (evaluate), or given the amount, find the time (solve with logs). One stop per scenario type on the check.

stops.title: Compound interest
stops.target: Use \(A(t) = P\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\). To find the amount, plug in \(t\). To find the time, plug in \(A\), isolate the power, and use logs.
stops.cold: A savings account starts with \$20,000 and earns 4% compounded quarterly. (a) How much is in the account after 5 years? (b) How long until it has \$30,000?
stops.coldPlain: A savings account starts with $20,000 and earns 4% compounded quarterly. (a) How much after 5 years? (b) How long until it has $30,000?
stops.mistake: Using n instead of nt in the exponent, or forgetting to divide by P before taking logs.
stops.again: \$15,000 at 3% compounded monthly. (a) Amount after 8 years? (b) When will it reach \$20,000?
stops.stretch: If the same \$15,000 earned 3% compounded continuously, \(A = Pe^{rt}\), how much would it be after 8 years?
stops.stretchA: \(15{,}000e^{0.24} \approx \$19{,}068.74\), a little more than monthly compounding (that is \(e\) from EL1).
stops.reflect: Which question uses logs, and why?

stops.title: Population growth
stops.target: For \(P(t) = a \cdot b^t\): \(a\) is the starting population. If you are told the population at a later time, use it to find \(b\) first, then answer the questions.
stops.cold: A colony starts with 2,000 bacteria; after 3 days there are 6,750. (a) Find \(b\). (b) How many after 7 days? (c) When will there be 100,000?
stops.coldPlain: A colony starts with 2,000 bacteria; after 3 days there are 6,750. (a) Find b. (b) How many after 7 days? (c) When will there be 100,000?
stops.solution: (a) Plug in the known point: 2000 b^3 = 6750, so b^3 = 3.375 and b = cube root of 3.375 = 1.5. (b) P(7) = 2000(1.5)^7, about 34,172. (c) 2000(1.5)^t = 100000 gives 1.5^t = 50, so t = ln 50 / ln 1.5, about 9.65 days.
stops.mistake: Finding b by dividing 6750 by 2000 (that gives b^3, not b).
stops.again: 300 deer grow to 4,800 after 4 years. Find \(b\), the population after 6 years, and when there will be 10,000 deer.
stops.reflect: Why do you need a root to find \(b\)?

stops.title: Depreciation
stops.target: A value that loses \(r\) per year follows \(V(t) = A(1 - r)^t\). The factor is less than 1, so the graph decreases.
stops.cold: A car is worth \$40,000 and depreciates 5% per year. (a) Value after 6 years? (b) When will it be worth \$20,000?
stops.coldPlain: A car is worth $40,000 and depreciates 5% per year. (a) Value after 6 years? (b) When will it be worth $20,000?
stops.solution: Losing 5% keeps 95%: factor 0.95. (a) 40000(0.95)^6, about $29,403.68. (b) Divide by 40000: 0.95^t = 0.5, so t = ln 0.5 / ln 0.95, about 13.51 years. Both logs are negative, so the answer comes out positive.
stops.again: A boat worth \$55,000 depreciates 3.5% per year. Value after 10 years? When will it be worth \$35,000?

stops.title: Half-life
stops.target: For radioactive decay, \(A(t) = A_0\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/h}\), where \(h\) is the half-life: every \(h\) units of time, half is left.
stops.cold: Cesium-137 has a half-life of 30 years. A sample has 600 micrograms. (a) How much is left after 90 years? (b) When will 18.75 micrograms be left?
stops.coldPlain: Cesium-137 has a half-life of 30 years. A sample has 600 micrograms. (a) How much after 90 years? (b) When will 18.75 micrograms be left?
stops.coldA:
\(A(t) = 600\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/30}\).
(a) 90 years is 3 half-lives: \(600 \cdot \tfrac{1}{8} = 75\) µg.
(b) \(\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/30} = \tfrac{18.75}{600} = \tfrac{1}{32}\), so \(\tfrac{t}{30} = 5\) and \(t = 150\) years.[[graph:HL]]
stops.solution: (a) t/30 = 3, so (1/2)^3 = 1/8 and 600/8 = 75. (b) Divide by 600: (1/2)^(t/30) = 1/32 = (1/2)^5, so t/30 = 5 and t = 150 years. When the fraction is not a power of 1/2, use logs.
stops.mistake: Multiplying 90 by 1/2 instead of counting half-lives.
stops.again: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years. A 200 g sample: how much after 11,460 years? When will 12.5 g be left?
stops.stretch: When will the cesium sample have 100 micrograms?
stops.reflect: How can you sometimes solve a half-life problem without logs?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same format as the EL7 CheckIt: one scenario, one "find the amount" and one "find the time" question.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Set up the model, then evaluate it for a given time and solve it for a given amount.
stops.cold:
A certificate of deposit has \$25,000 in it initially and earns 4.5%, compounded semiannually, modeled by \(A(t) = P\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\).
(a) How much is in the account after 12 years?
(b) How long will it take for the account to have \$40,000?
stops.coldPlain: A CD has $25,000 initially at 4.5% compounded semiannually, A(t) = P(1 + r/n)^(nt). (a) Amount after 12 years? (b) How long until $40,000?
stops.mistake: Using n = 1 for semiannual (it is 2), or not dividing by P first.
stops.again: Algae grow exponentially, \(P(t) = a \cdot b^t\). There are 3,000 initially and 12,000 after 2 days. (a) How many after 6 days? (b) How long until there are 1,000,000?
stops.reflect: How do you know which question needs logs?
